Technical Specifications
1. Introduction

1.1 Executive Summary

1.1.1 Brief Overview Of The Project

ShopAdmin is a comprehensive multi-store order management system designed to streamline the administration of multiple React-based ecommerce stores from a single, unified dashboard. Built on Next.js 14 with TypeScript, the application leverages modern web technologies including Tailwind CSS, Chakra UI, Node.js with Express, and Prisma ORM with PostgreSQL to deliver a robust, scalable solution for ecommerce management.

1.1.2 Core Business Problem Being Solved

The project addresses the critical challenge faced by businesses operating multiple online stores: the complexity and inefficiency of managing orders, inventory, and customer data across disparate ecommerce platforms. Traditional approaches require administrators to log into multiple systems, manually reconcile data, and perform repetitive tasks across different interfaces, leading to operational inefficiencies, increased error rates, and poor customer service response times.

1.1.3 Key Stakeholders And Users

Stakeholder GroupPrimary RoleKey Interests
Store AdministratorsDaily operations managementCentralized order processing, real-time updates, streamlined workflows
Business OwnersStrategic oversightAnalytics, performance metrics, scalability, cost efficiency
Customer Service TeamsOrder support and resolutionQuick access to order details, status updates, customer communication tools

1.1.4 Expected Business Impact And Value Proposition

The ShopAdmin platform delivers measurable business value through operational efficiency gains, reduced administrative overhead, and improved customer satisfaction. Key benefits include:

  • Operational Efficiency: Centralized management reduces time spent switching between systems by up to 70%
  • Error Reduction: Unified data management minimizes manual data entry errors and inconsistencies
  • Scalability: Modern serverless architecture with Prisma ORM enables rapid scaling from zero to thousands of requests per second
  • Cost Optimization: Consolidated tooling reduces licensing costs and training requirements

1.2 System Overview

1.2.1 Project Context

Business Context And Market Positioning

The ecommerce landscape has evolved rapidly, with businesses increasingly adopting multi-channel strategies to reach diverse customer segments. Next.js popularity has increased from 13.52% in 2022 to 16.67% in 2023, while 43% of developers believe TypeScript will overtake JavaScript as the new standard, indicating strong market alignment with the chosen technology stack.

Current System Limitations

Existing solutions typically suffer from:

  • Fragmented data across multiple platforms
  • Lack of real-time synchronization
  • Limited customization capabilities
  • Poor integration between different store systems
  • Inadequate reporting and analytics consolidation

Integration With Existing Enterprise Landscape

ShopAdmin is designed as a centralized hub that integrates with existing React-based ecommerce stores through standardized APIs. The platform supports secure API endpoints for third-party service integration, authentication handling, and webhook processing, ensuring seamless connectivity with current enterprise infrastructure.

1.2.2 High-level Description

Primary System Capabilities

CapabilityDescriptionTechnical Implementation
Multi-Store ManagementCentralized dashboard for multiple storesNext.js 14 with stable Server Actions and full end-to-end TypeScript type-safety
Real-Time Order ProcessingLive order status updates and notificationsWebSocket integration with Express.js backend
Analytics and ReportingComprehensive business intelligencePrisma Accelerate with global caching and connection pooling
Export FunctionalityData export in multiple formatsServer-side processing with type-safe operations

Major System Components

The system architecture follows a modern monorepo structure with clear separation of concerns:

Core Technical Approach

The application provides a TypeScript-first development experience with enhanced type safety through the Next.js App Router. Prisma ORM serves as the next-generation database layer, providing type-safety, automated migrations, and an intuitive data model for PostgreSQL.

Measurable Objectives

Critical Success Factors

1.3 Scope

1.3.1 In-scope

Core Features And Functionalities

Feature CategorySpecific Capabilities
Order ManagementCRUD operations, status tracking, bulk updates, search and filtering
Multi-Store IntegrationStore registration, API key management, data synchronization
Analytics DashboardReal-time metrics, trend analysis, custom reports, export functionality
User ManagementRole-based access control, authentication, audit logging

Primary User Workflows

  • Store Administrator Workflow: Login → Dashboard Overview → Order Management → Status Updates → Analytics Review
  • Business Owner Workflow: Login → Executive Dashboard → Performance Analytics → Store Comparison → Strategic Planning
  • Customer Service Workflow: Login → Order Search → Customer Communication → Issue Resolution → Documentation

Essential Integrations

  • React ecommerce store APIs
  • Payment gateway webhooks
  • Email notification services
  • File export systems (CSV, PDF, Excel)

Key Technical Requirements

  • Latest Chakra UI version 3.27.0 with responsive and accessible React components
  • Most popular Node.js and TypeScript ORM with human-readable schema and auto-generated migrations
  • Built-in connection pooling and global caching for serverless applications

1.3.2 Implementation Boundaries

System Boundaries

The ShopAdmin system operates as a centralized management layer that interfaces with external ecommerce stores through standardized APIs. The system boundary includes the admin dashboard, API gateway, database layer, and integration endpoints.

User Groups Covered

  • Store administrators (primary users)
  • Business owners and managers
  • Customer service representatives
  • System administrators

Geographic/market Coverage

Initial deployment targets English-speaking markets with plans for internationalization in future phases.

Data Domains Included

  • Order data (transactions, items, customer information)
  • Store configuration and metadata
  • User accounts and permissions
  • Analytics and reporting data

1.3.3 Out-of-scope

Explicitly Excluded Features/capabilities

  • Direct customer-facing ecommerce functionality
  • Payment processing (handled by existing store systems)
  • Inventory management beyond order tracking
  • Customer relationship management (CRM) features
  • Marketing automation tools
  • Mobile application development

Future Phase Considerations

  • Advanced AI-powered analytics and forecasting
  • Mobile companion application
  • Advanced workflow automation
  • Third-party marketplace integrations (Amazon, eBay)
  • Multi-language support and localization

Integration Points Not Covered

  • Legacy non-React ecommerce platforms
  • Enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems
  • Advanced accounting software integration
  • Supply chain management systems

Unsupported Use Cases

  • Real-time inventory synchronization across stores
  • Complex multi-currency transaction processing
  • Advanced fraud detection and prevention
  • Automated marketing campaign management
  • Customer loyalty program management

3. Technology Stack

3.1 Programming Languages

3.1.1 Frontend Languages

LanguageVersionPlatformJustification
TypeScript5.3+Frontend (Next.js)Enhanced type safety with Next.js 14 stable Server Actions and full end-to-end TypeScript type-safety. TypeScript is the current industry standard for creating JavaScript applications, enhancing JavaScript code by adding types for building large-scale products that are more maintainable and less error-prone
JavaScript (ES2022+)ES2022+Runtime SupportBuilt on React canary channel which is stable for frameworks to adopt new features

3.1.2 Backend Languages

LanguageVersionPlatformJustification
TypeScript5.3+Backend (Node.js/Express)Express v5 drops support for Node.js versions before v18, enabling more stable and maintainable continuous integration, adopting new language and runtime features
SQLPostgreSQL DialectDatabase QueriesExecute SQL queries directly against database without losing benefits of Prisma's type-checking and auto-completion. TypedSQL leverages capabilities of Prisma Client to write raw SQL queries that are type-checked at compile time

3.1.3 Selection Criteria

Type Safety Requirements: Prisma ORM provides the strongest type-safety guarantees of all ORMs in the TypeScript ecosystem

Performance Considerations: Next.js 14.2 Turbopack Release Candidate with 99.8% of integration tests passing for next dev --turbo

Ecosystem Compatibility: Chakra UI works with Next.js RSC (React Server Components)

5. System Architecture

5.1 High-level Architecture

5.1.1 System Overview

The ShopAdmin system employs a modern monorepo architecture managed by Yarn workspaces, housing multiple projects in a single repository to enable seamless code sharing, streamlined dependency management, and improved collaboration. The architecture follows a monolithic approach where the entire application is built as a single, cohesive unit, with all pages, components, and API routes managed within the same project structure.

The system is built on Next.js by Vercel as the full-stack React framework for the web, leveraging the latest React features, including Server Components and Actions. The backend utilizes Express as a minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework that provides a robust set of features for web and mobile applications, while Prisma ORM provides modern serverless architecture with tight integration, creating a Postgres variant that scales as fast as your ideas.

The architectural style emphasizes separation of files and classes into components that can change independently without affecting other components, which is what Clean Architecture is all about. This approach ensures layered architectures that make it easier to write quality code that will perform better, is easy to maintain, and has fewer dependencies as the project grows.

Key architectural principles include:

  • Type Safety First: Full end-to-end TypeScript integration with compile-time validation
  • Serverless Scalability: Architecture that scales from zero to thousands of requests per second
  • Real-time Communication: WebSocket-based live updates with pub/sub patterns
  • Data Consistency: ACID-compliant transactions with automated rollback mechanisms
  • Modular Design: Clear separation of concerns with independent component evolution

5.1.2 Core Components Table

Component NamePrimary ResponsibilityKey DependenciesIntegration Points
Next.js FrontendUser interface, routing, server-side renderingReact 18+, Chakra UI v3, Tailwind CSS v4Express API, WebSocket server, authentication middleware
Express API ServerBusiness logic, request handling, data validationTypeScript 5.3+, middleware stack, route handlersPrisma ORM, WebSocket server, external store APIs
Prisma ORM LayerDatabase abstraction, type-safe queries, migrationsPostgreSQL 18+, connection pooling, schema managementExpress controllers, background jobs, cache layer
WebSocket ServerReal-time communication, event broadcasting, connection managementSocket.io, pub/sub patterns, connection poolingExpress server, Redis cache, client subscriptions

5.1.3 Data Flow Description

The primary data flow follows a publish/subscribe pattern where pages subscribe to only those events they can use, and call the view update logic as those events come in. Server Actions enable running server code by calling a function, providing seamless integration between client and server operations.

Data originates from external React ecommerce stores through standardized REST APIs, flows through the Express middleware stack for validation and transformation, then persists to PostgreSQL via Prisma ORM's type-safe queries. Query-level cache strategies serve data fast from the global edge network, with unikernel-powered microVMs running on bare-metal servers to maximize Postgres performance.

Real-time updates utilize WebSocket protocol's persistent, real-time, full-duplex communication over a single TCP socket connection, with only two agendas: to open up a handshake and to help the data transfer. The pub/sub messaging paradigm allows publishers to send data through channels that subscribers listen to, providing highly efficient, robust communication that scales with no effort.

The system implements type-safe database access with an intuitive API while maintaining transparency and control over database operations. Data transformation occurs at multiple layers: API normalization for external store integration, business logic processing in Express controllers, and UI state management in React components.

5.2.1 Next.js Frontend Application

Purpose and Responsibilities
The frontend serves as the primary user interface for multi-store order management, providing a responsive admin dashboard with real-time updates. It creates routes using the file system, including support for advanced routing patterns and UI layouts, while adding components without sending additional client-side JavaScript, built on the latest React features.

Technologies and Frameworks

  • Chakra UI provides accessible React components for building high-quality web apps and design systems, with over 25 new components in version 3

Key Interfaces and APIs

  • Server Actions for form submissions and data mutations
  • WebSocket client connections for real-time updates
  • REST API integration for external store communication
  • Authentication middleware for secure access control

Data Persistence Requirements

  • Client-side state management for UI components
  • Session storage for user authentication
  • Local caching for frequently accessed data
  • Real-time synchronization with server state

Scaling Considerations
Turbopack, an incremental bundler optimized for JavaScript and TypeScript written in Rust and built into Next.js, provides enhanced build performance. The application supports horizontal scaling through serverless deployment patterns and edge network distribution.

5.2.2 Express Api Server

Purpose and Responsibilities
The Express server handles all business logic, API routing, middleware processing, and external integrations. It uses the factory pattern by only exporting the factory function, allowing for clean application instantiation. Middleware implements the Chain of Responsibility pattern, where requests must pass conditions inside each middleware function.

Technologies and Frameworks

  • Express.js remains the de facto standard for Node.js web applications due to its minimalist philosophy, mature ecosystem, performance, flexibility, and gentle learning curve
  • TypeScript with the latest tsx runner for robust type safety, ESLint's new flat config for linting, and Prettier for consistent formatting
  • Clean Architecture standards that develop layered architectures making it easier to write quality code that performs better and is easy to maintain

Key Interfaces and APIs

  • WebSocket server integration for real-time communication
  • External store API connectors with OAuth 2.0
  • Middleware stack for authentication, validation, and error handling

Data Persistence Requirements

  • Session management for user authentication
  • API key storage with encryption
  • Request/response logging for audit trails
  • Cache management for performance optimization

Scaling Considerations
Node.js shines in handling many connections by utilizing an event-driven, non-blocking architecture, allowing it to serve multiple clients without getting bogged down. The server supports clustering, load balancing, and microservices decomposition for horizontal scaling.

5.2.3 Prisma Orm And Database Layer

Purpose and Responsibilities
Prisma ORM provides fully type-safe queries, easy schema management, migrations and auto-completion. It provides a powerful and intuitive way to interact with PostgreSQL databases, with its type-safe client, schema-based approach, and rich feature set making it excellent for projects of all sizes.

Technologies and Frameworks

  • Prisma ORM provides a high-level overview of technical components, with every project starting with a Prisma schema file for thorough database integration
  • PostgreSQL data source connector connects Prisma ORM to a PostgreSQL database server, with the connector containing a database driver responsible for connecting to your database
  • Prisma Postgres uses a unique architecture deployed on bare metal servers using unikernels (hyper-specialized operating systems) to deliver unmatched efficiency, safety and ease of use

Key Interfaces and APIs

  • Auto-generated and type-safe query builder that can be imported and instantiated for database operations
  • Schema-first development with automated migrations
  • Connection pooling and query optimization
  • Transaction management with ACID compliance

Data Persistence Requirements

  • Type-safe database layers that eliminate runtime errors and accelerate development through auto-generated schemas, reducing development time by 50% while providing enterprise-grade performance
  • Automated backup and recovery procedures
  • Data encryption for sensitive information
  • Audit logging for compliance requirements

Scaling Considerations
Blazing-fast performance from the first request, scaling to thousands per second with serverless architecture done right. The system supports read replicas, connection pooling, and query-level caching for optimal performance.

5.2.4 Websocket Real-time Communication

Purpose and Responsibilities
WebSocket provides standardized communication protocol enabling simultaneous two-way communication over a single TCP connection, with full-duplex capabilities that distinguish it from HTTP. The Pub/Sub pattern allows publishers to send messages to channels while subscribers receive messages, enabling decoupled communication ideal for real-time applications.

Technologies and Frameworks

  • Node.js v21 enhanced WebSocket API using the Undici library, with v22.4.0 marking the WebSocket API as stable for production use
  • Socket.io abstracts low-level WebSocket details and provides a simple API for real-time messaging with automatic reconnection and reliability
  • Redis as an in-memory data store providing pub/sub messaging paradigm for efficient communication between distributed instances

Key Interfaces and APIs

  • WebSocket connection management with authentication
  • Channel subscription and message broadcasting
  • Heartbeat mechanisms for connection health monitoring
  • Event-driven message routing and filtering

Data Persistence Requirements

  • Connection state management across server instances
  • Message queuing for offline clients
  • Session recovery for connection interruptions
  • Event logging for debugging and analytics

Scaling Considerations
Distributed architecture eliminates concerns about which instance holds socket connections, providing robust solutions that handle the vast majority of cases. The system supports horizontal scaling through Redis pub/sub and connection pooling strategies.

5.3 Technical Decisions

5.3.1 Architecture Style Decisions And Tradeoffs

The selection of a monorepo architecture over microservices represents a strategic decision optimized for development velocity and operational simplicity. Using a monorepo ensures consistent structure and organization, allows scaling by adding new packages without breaking existing code, and enables caching and performance optimizations that improve build times.

Monolithic vs Microservices Analysis

Decision FactorMonolithic ChoiceMicroservices AlternativeRationale
Development ComplexityLower initial complexityHigher operational overheadTeam size and expertise favor unified development
Deployment StrategySingle deployment unitIndependent service deploymentSimplified CI/CD pipeline reduces operational burden
Data ConsistencyACID transactionsEventual consistency patternsOrder management requires strong consistency guarantees
Technology StackUnified TypeScript ecosystemPolyglot architecture flexibilityType safety benefits outweigh language diversity

Framework Selection Rationale

Next.js has become the go-to choice for many developers with features such as server-side rendering, static site generation, and API routes, with its true power lying in flexibility that allows creating a wide variety of application architectures. The framework selection prioritizes developer experience, performance, and ecosystem maturity over architectural complexity.

5.3.2 Communication Pattern Choices

The hybrid communication approach combines REST APIs for traditional CRUD operations with WebSockets for real-time updates, optimizing for both reliability and performance. WebSocket protocol solves HTTP's drawbacks by offering full-duplex communication mechanism, helping developers build real-time apps with persistent, real-time communication over a single TCP socket connection.

REST vs WebSocket Decision Matrix

Protocol Selection Justification

WebSocket provides persistent, stateful connections allowing both client and server to send messages at any time, making it great for realtime communication while facing new challenges. The decision to use WebSockets for real-time features while maintaining REST for standard operations provides optimal performance characteristics for each use case.

5.3.3 Data Storage Solution Rationale

PostgreSQL selection over alternative databases reflects requirements for ACID compliance, complex queries, and mature ecosystem support. Prisma ORM strikes an excellent balance by providing type-safe database access with an intuitive API while maintaining transparency and control, making it refreshing and powerful for building APIs.

Database Technology Comparison

ScalabilityVertical + horizontalHorizontal-firstVertical-focused

}

6.2 Backend Api Architecture

6.2.1 Express.js Server Structure

The backend architecture utilizes Express.js latest version: 5.1.0, last published: 6 months ago. Starting with this version, Express supports Node.js 18.x, providing a robust foundation for API development with modern JavaScript features.

Server Architecture Components

ComponentTechnologyResponsibilityImplementation Details
HTTP ServerExpress.js 5.1.0Request handlingExpress philosophy is to provide small, robust tooling for HTTP servers
Middleware StackExpress MiddlewareRequest processingAuthentication, validation, error handling
Route HandlersTypeScriptBusiness logicType-safe request/response handling

API Route Structure

// Express v5 Route Handler with TypeScript
import express, { Request, Response, NextFunction } from 'express';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

const app = express();
const prisma = new PrismaClient();

// Middleware stack
app.use(express.json());
app.use(authenticationMiddleware);
app.use(validationMiddleware);

// Order management routes
app.get('/api/orders', async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  try {
    const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({
      include: { store: true, items: true }
    });
    res.json(orders);
  } catch (error) {
    next(error);
  }
});

// Error handling middleware
app.use((error: Error, req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {

// Prisma Schema Definition
generator client {
  provider = "prisma-client-js"
}

datasource db {
  provider = "postgresql"
  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
}

model Store {
  id          String   @id @default(cuid())
  name        String
  apiKey      String   @unique
  apiUrl      String
  isActive    Boolean  @default(true)
  orders      Order[]
  createdAt   DateTime @default(now())
  updatedAt   DateTime @updatedAt
  
  @@map("stores")
}

model Order {
  id          String      @id @default(cuid())
  storeId     String
  store       Store       @relation(fields: [storeId], references: [id])
  orderNumber String
  status      OrderStatus
  totalAmount Decimal
  items       OrderItem[]
  createdAt   DateTime    @default(now())
  updatedAt   DateTime    @updatedAt
  
  @@map("orders")
}

enum OrderStatus {
  PENDING
  PROCESSING
  SHIPPED
  DELIVERED
  CANCELLED
}

Validation and Security Middleware

import { z } from 'zod';
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';
import rateLimit from 'express-rate-limit';

// Input validation schema
const orderSchema = z.object({
  storeId: z.string().cuid(),
  orderNumber: z.string().min(1),
  status: z.enum(['PENDING', 'PROCESSING', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED']),
  totalAmount: z.number().positive(),
  items: z.array(z.object({
    name: z.string(),
    quantity: z.number().int().positive(),
    price: z.number().positive()
  }))
});

// Authentication middleware
const authenticateToken = (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
  const authHeader = req.headers['authorization'];
  const token = authHeader && authHeader.split(' ')[1];

  if (!token) {
    return res.sendStatus(401);
  }

  jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET!, (err, user) => {
    if (err) return res.sendStatus(403);
    req.user = user;
    next();
  });
};

// Rate limiting
const limiter = rateLimit({
  windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, // 15 minutes
  max: 100, // limit each IP to 100 requests per windowMs
  message: 'Too many requests from this IP'
});

app.use('/api/', limiter);

// Server-side WebSocket handling
import { Server } from 'socket.io';
import { createAdapter } from '@socket.io/redis-adapter';
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const io = new Server(httpServer, {
  cors: {
    origin: process.env.FRONTEND_URL,
    credentials: true
  }
});

// Redis adapter for scaling
const pubClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const subClient = pubClient.duplicate();
io.adapter(createAdapter(pubClient, subClient));

// Authentication middleware
io.use(async (socket, next) => {
  try {
    const token = socket.handshake.auth.token;
    const user = await verifyToken(token);
    socket.userId = user.id;
    socket.userStores = user.storeAccess;
    next();
  } catch (error) {
    next(new Error('Authentication failed'));
  }
});

// Connection handling
io.on('connection', (socket) => {
  console.log(`User ${socket.userId} connected`);
  
  // Join store-specific rooms
  socket.userStores.forEach(storeId => {
    socket.join(`store:${storeId}`);
  });
  
  // Handle order updates
  socket.on('order:subscribe', (orderId) => {
    socket.join(`order:${orderId}`);
  });
  
  socket.on('disconnect', () => {
    console.log(`User ${socket.userId} disconnected`);
  });
});

// Event broadcasting
export const broadcastOrderUpdate = (orderId: string, orderData: any) => {
  io.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('order:updated', {
    orderId,
    data: orderData,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
  });
};

6.4.3 Client-side Real-time Integration

The frontend integrates WebSocket communication seamlessly with React components, providing real-time updates without disrupting user interactions or application state.

React WebSocket Integration

// Custom hook for WebSocket connection
import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
import { io, Socket } from 'socket.io-client';

export const useWebSocket = (token: string) => {
  const [socket, setSocket] = useState<Socket | null>(null);
  const [connected, setConnected] = useState(false);

  useEffect(() => {
    const socketInstance = io(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_WS_URL!, {
      auth: { token },
      autoConnect: true
    });

    socketInstance.on('connect', () => {
      setConnected(true);
      console.log('WebSocket connected');
    });

    socketInstance.on('disconnect', () => {
      setConnected(false);
      console.log('WebSocket disconnected');
    });

    setSocket(socketInstance);

    return () => {
      socketInstance.disconnect();
    };
  }, [token]);

  return { socket, connected };
};

// Order list component with real-time updates
export const OrderList = () => {
  const [orders, setOrders] = useState<Order[]>([]);
  const { socket } = useWebSocket(userToken);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!socket) return;

    // Listen for order updates
    socket.on('order:updated', (event) => {
      setOrders(prevOrders => 
        prevOrders.map(order => 
          order.id === event.orderId 
            ? { ...order, ...event.data }
            : order
        )
      );
    });

    // Listen for new orders
    socket.on('order:created', (event) => {
      setOrders(prevOrders => [event.data, ...prevOrders]);
    });

    return () => {
      socket.off('order:updated');
      socket.off('order:created');
    };
  }, [socket]);

  return (
    <div>
      {orders.map(order => (
        <OrderCard key={order.id} order={order} />
      ))}
    </div>
  );
};

Store Integration Implementation

// Abstract base class for store integrations
abstract class StoreAdapter {
  protected apiKey: string;
  protected baseUrl: string;
  protected rateLimiter: RateLimiter;

  constructor(config: StoreConfig) {
    this.apiKey = config.apiKey;
    this.baseUrl = config.baseUrl;
    this.rateLimiter = new RateLimiter(config.rateLimit);
  }

  abstract async fetchOrders(params: FetchOrdersParams): Promise<Order[]>;
  abstract async updateOrderStatus(orderId: string, status: OrderStatus): Promise<void>;
  abstract async validateConnection(): Promise<boolean>;

  protected async makeRequest<T>(endpoint: string, options: RequestOptions): Promise<T> {
    await this.rateLimiter.acquire();
    
    try {
      const response = await fetch(`${this.baseUrl}${endpoint}`, {
        ...options,
        headers: {
          'Authorization': `Bearer ${this.apiKey}`,
          'Content-Type': 'application/json',
          ...options.headers
        }
      });

      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new APIError(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${response.statusText}`);
      }

      return await response.json();
    } catch (error) {
      this.handleAPIError(error);
      throw error;
    }
  }
}

// Specific store implementation
class ShopifyAdapter extends StoreAdapter {
  async fetchOrders(params: FetchOrdersParams): Promise<Order[]> {
    const response = await this.makeRequest<ShopifyOrdersResponse>(
      '/admin/api/2023-10/orders.json',
      { method: 'GET' }
    );

    return response.orders.map(this.normalizeOrder);
  }

  private normalizeOrder(shopifyOrder: ShopifyOrder): Order {
    return {
      id: shopifyOrder.id.toString(),
      orderNumber: shopifyOrder.order_number,
      status: this.mapStatus(shopifyOrder.fulfillment_status),
      totalAmount: parseFloat(shopifyOrder.total_price),
      customerData: {
        name: `${shopifyOrder.customer.first_name} ${shopifyOrder.customer.last_name}`,
        email: shopifyOrder.customer.email
      },
      items: shopifyOrder.line_items.map(item => ({
        name: item.name,
        quantity: item.quantity,
        unitPrice: parseFloat(item.price),
        totalPrice: parseFloat(item.price) * item.quantity
      })),
      orderDate: new Date(shopifyOrder.created_at),
      createdAt: new Date(),
      updatedAt: new Date()
    };
  }
}

6.5.2 Webhook Processing System

ComponentResponsibilityTechnologySecurity Features

Webhook Processing Flow

Webhook Handler Implementation

// Webhook endpoint with signature verification
app.post('/webhooks/:storeId/orders', async (req, res) => {
  try {
    const { storeId } = req.params;
    const signature = req.headers['x-webhook-signature'] as string;
    const payload = req.body;

    // Verify webhook signature
    const store = await prisma.store.findUnique({
      where: { id: storeId }
    });

    if (!store || !verifyWebhookSignature(payload, signature, store.webhookSecret)) {
      return res.status(401).json({ error: 'Invalid signature' });
    }

    // Enqueue for processing
    await webhookQueue.add('process-order-webhook', {
      storeId,
      payload,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
    }, {
      attempts: 3,
      backoff: {
        type: 'exponential',
        delay: 2000
      }
    });

    res.status(200).json({ received: true });
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Webhook processing error:', error);
    res.status(500).json({ error: 'Internal server error' });
  }
});

// Queue processor
webhookQueue.process('process-order-webhook', async (job) => {
  const { storeId, payload } = job.data;
  
  try {
    // Get store adapter
    const adapter = await getStoreAdapter(storeId);
    
    // Normalize webhook data
    const orderData = adapter.normalizeWebhookPayload(payload);
    
    // Update database with transaction
    await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
      const existingOrder = await tx.order.findUnique({
        where: { 
          storeId_orderNumber: {
            storeId,
            orderNumber: orderData.orderNumber
          }
        }
      });

      if (existingOrder) {
        // Update existing order
        await tx.order.update({
          where: { id: existingOrder.id },
          data: orderData
        });
      } else {
        // Create new order
        await tx.order.create({
          data: {
            ...orderData,
            storeId
          }
        });
      }
    });

    // Broadcast real-time update
    broadcastOrderUpdate(orderData.id, orderData);
    
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Webhook processing failed:', error);
    throw error; // Will trigger retry
  }
});

Email Service Integration

// Email service abstraction
interface EmailService {
  sendOrderNotification(order: Order, recipient: string): Promise<void>;
  sendSystemAlert(alert: SystemAlert, recipients: string[]): Promise<void>;
}

class SendGridEmailService implements EmailService {
  private client: SendGridClient;

  constructor(apiKey: string) {
    this.client = new SendGridClient(apiKey);
  }

  async sendOrderNotification(order: Order, recipient: string): Promise<void> {
    const msg = {
      to: recipient,
      from: process.env.FROM_EMAIL!,
      templateId: 'order-notification-template',
      dynamicTemplateData: {
        orderNumber: order.orderNumber,
        status: order.status,
        totalAmount: order.totalAmount,
        items: order.items
      }
    };

    await this.client.send(msg);
  }

  async sendSystemAlert(alert: SystemAlert, recipients: string[]): Promise<void> {
    const msg = {
      to: recipients,
      from: process.env.SYSTEM_EMAIL!,
      subject: `System Alert: ${alert.title}`,
      html: `
        <h2>${alert.title}</h2>
        <p><strong>Severity:</strong> ${alert.severity}</p>
        <p><strong>Description:</strong> ${alert.description}</p>
        <p><strong>Time:</strong> ${alert.timestamp}</p>
      `
    };

    await this.client.sendMultiple(msg);
  }
}

// Service factory
export const createEmailService = (): EmailService => {
  const provider = process.env.EMAIL_PROVIDER || 'sendgrid';
  
  switch (provider) {
    case 'sendgrid':
      return new SendGridEmailService(process.env.SENDGRID_API_KEY!);
    case 'ses':
      return new AWSEmailService(process.env.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID!);
    default:
      throw new Error(`Unsupported email provider: ${provider}`);
  }
};

This comprehensive system components design provides a robust, scalable, and maintainable architecture for the ShopAdmin multi-store order management platform, leveraging the latest technologies and best practices for modern web application development.

Based on my analysis of the ShopAdmin project requirements and current technology trends, I need to address whether this system requires a distributed services architecture or if it should remain monolithic.

6.1 Core Services Architecture

Core Services Architecture is not applicable for this system as a distributed microservices approach. The ShopAdmin multi-store order management system is optimally designed as a monolithic architecture where the entire application is built as a single, cohesive unit, with all pages, components, and API routes managed within the same project.

6.1.1 Architectural Decision Rationale

The decision to implement a monolithic architecture over microservices is based on several key factors:

Decision FactorMonolithic AdvantageMicroservices DrawbackImpact on ShopAdmin
Development ComplexitySimplified development where developers can focus on building features without worrying about integrating different servicesIncreased complexity managing multiple services with robust communication and coordination, plus operational overhead deploying and maintaining multiple servicesSingle developer/small team efficiency
Deployment StrategyEasier deployment with single build and deploy process reducing complexityComplex orchestration requirementsSimplified CI/CD pipeline
Data ConsistencyACID transactions with PostgreSQLEventual consistency challengesOrder management requires strong consistency
Technology IntegrationNextJS combines ease of unified codebase with modern web technologies' flexibility and performance enhancementsTechnology fragmentationUnified TypeScript ecosystem

6.1.2 Modern Monolithic Architecture Benefits

NextJS represents a compelling evolution of the monolithic paradigm, adapting it to meet the needs of today's developers and users. The framework provides several advantages that make monolithic architecture viable for modern applications:

Performance Optimizations

  • Server-side rendering (SSR) and static site generation (SSG) ensure applications are fast, SEO-friendly, and capable of delivering dynamic content efficiently
  • Built-in API routes eliminate the need for separate backend services, allowing developers to create full-fledged applications with ease

Development Experience

  • Small team or even single developer can create high-quality, scalable application that can handle large number of users and traffic
  • Postpones the inevitable scale point for teams to outgrow monolithic architecture

6.1.3 Scalability Through Modular Monolithic Design

While avoiding microservices complexity, the system implements a modular monolithic architecture that provides scalability benefits:

Modular Structure Within Monolith

Modular Benefits

  • Clean structure ensures adding features without project collapsing under its own weight, with code easier to understand and manage
  • Architecture separates different parts of application into logical directories, making it easy to find and understand code, and easy to add new features without affecting other parts

6.1.4 Horizontal Scaling Strategy

The monolithic architecture supports horizontal scaling through proven patterns:

Scaling Approach

Scaling DimensionImplementationTechnologyBenefits
Application InstancesLoad balancer + multiple app instancesNext.js deploymentLoad balancing distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers, ensuring no single server becomes overwhelmed
Database ScalingRead replicas + connection poolingPostgreSQL + PrismaBuilt-in connection pooling for serverless applications
Caching LayerMulti-level caching strategyRedis + Prisma AccelerateQuery-level cache strategies with global edge network
Real-time CommunicationWebSocket clusteringSocket.io with Redis adapterDistributed WebSocket connections across instances

Scaling Architecture

6.1.5 Performance Optimization Techniques

The monolithic architecture leverages modern performance optimization strategies:

Application-Level Optimizations

  • Clean Architecture develops layered architectures making it easier to write quality code that performs better, is easy to maintain, and has fewer dependencies as project grows
  • Asynchronous programming leveraging promises, async/await ensures application remains responsive and efficient, especially when dealing with I/O operations

Infrastructure Optimizations

  • Scalable architecture allows application to handle increased workloads without sacrificing performance, ensuring application remains responsive and reliable
  • Scalable architecture helps optimize resource usage and reduce operational costs

6.1.6 Migration Path Consideration

The modular monolithic design provides a clear migration path if microservices become necessary:

Future Microservices Transition

Migration Strategy

  • Modular approach makes it easier to convert into microservices when needed
  • Modularizing doesn't require huge rewrite — it's incremental step that improves maintainability without sacrificing simplicity of single deployment

6.1.7 When To Consider Microservices

The system should consider transitioning to microservices only when specific conditions are met:

Transition Triggers

  • Modules start behaving like independent products with distinct business logic, databases, or user bases; hitting scalability bottlenecks where one team's feature brings down entire deployment; needing independent deployment cycles
  • Almost all successful microservice stories have started with monolith that got too big and was broken up; cases built as microservice system from scratch have ended up in serious trouble

Current Assessment
The ShopAdmin system does not meet these transition criteria:

  • Single business domain (order management)
  • Unified data model requirements
  • Small development team
  • Shared authentication and authorization needs
  • Strong consistency requirements for financial data

6.1.8 Conclusion

The ShopAdmin multi-store order management system is optimally architected as a modern monolithic application leveraging Next.js, Express.js, and PostgreSQL. This approach provides:

  1. Simplified Development: Single codebase with unified technology stack
  2. Strong Consistency: ACID transactions for order and financial data
  3. Performance: Modern optimizations without distributed system overhead
  4. Scalability: Horizontal scaling through load balancing and caching
  5. Maintainability: Modular structure within monolithic deployment
  6. Future Flexibility: Clear migration path to microservices if needed

Implementing Clean Architecture in monolithic projects saves significant time in development of new features, testability of system, and general maintenance of components, providing such robust service that teams can focus on shipping.

6.2.1.3 Indexing Strategy

The indexing strategy leverages PostgreSQL 18's "skip scan" lookups on multicolumn B-tree indexes that improve execution time for queries that omit an = condition on one or more prefix index columns and parallel builds for GIN indexes for optimal query performance.

Index Design Matrix

Index TypeUse CasePerformance BenefitImplementation
B-treePrimary keys, foreign keys, range queriesHandle equality and range queries on data that can be sorted, with BETWEEN and IN operationsDefault for most columns
GINJSONB data, full-text search, arraysInverted indexes appropriate for data values that contain multiple component valuesConfiguration data, search
PartialActive records onlyReduced index size and maintenanceStatus-based filtering
CompositeMulti-column queriesSingle index for complex queriesStore + order combinations

Strategic Index Implementation

-- Primary B-tree indexes for core operations
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_store_id ON orders(store_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_order_date ON orders(order_date DESC);

-- Composite indexes for common query patterns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_store_status_date ON orders(store_id, status, order_date DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_product ON order_items(order_id, product_id);

-- GIN indexes for JSONB and full-text search
CREATE INDEX idx_stores_configuration ON stores USING GIN (configuration);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_data ON orders USING GIN (customer_data);

-- Full-text search index for order search
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_search ON orders 
USING GIN (to_tsvector('english', order_number || ' ' || (customer_data->>'name')));

-- Partial indexes for active records
CREATE INDEX idx_active_stores ON stores (created_at)

-- Create partitioned orders table
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    store_id UUID NOT NULL,
    order_number VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    status order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
    total_amount DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
    customer_data JSONB NOT NULL,

    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT NOW()
) PARTITION BY RANGE (order_date);

-- Create monthly partitions
CREATE TABLE orders_2024_01 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2024-02-01');

CREATE TABLE orders_2024_02 PARTITION OF orders
    FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-02-01') TO ('2024-03-01');

-- Automated partition management
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION create_monthly_partition(table_name text, start_date date)
RETURNS void AS $$
DECLARE
    partition_name text;
    end_date date;
BEGIN
    partition_name := table_name || '_' || to_char(start_date, 'YYYY_MM');
    end_date := start_date + interval '1 month';
    
    EXECUTE format('CREATE TABLE %I PARTITION OF %I
                    FOR VALUES FROM (%L) TO (%L)',
                   partition_name, table_name, start_date, end_date);
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Automated archival procedure
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION archive_old_orders()
RETURNS void AS $$
BEGIN
    -- Move orders older than 2 years to archive
    INSERT INTO orders_archive 
    SELECT * FROM orders 
    WHERE order_date < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years';
    
    -- Delete archived orders from main table
    DELETE FROM orders 
    WHERE order_date < NOW() - INTERVAL '2 years';
    
    -- Update statistics
    ANALYZE orders;
    ANALYZE orders_archive;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Audit trigger function
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION audit_trigger()
RETURNS TRIGGER AS $$
BEGIN
    INSERT INTO audit_log (
        table_name,
        operation,
        old_values,
        new_values,
        user_id,
        timestamp
    ) VALUES (
        TG_TABLE_NAME,
        TG_OP,
        CASE WHEN TG_OP = 'DELETE' THEN row_to_json(OLD) ELSE NULL END,
        CASE WHEN TG_OP IN ('INSERT', 'UPDATE') THEN row_to_json(NEW) ELSE NULL END,
        current_setting('app.user_id', true),
        NOW()
    );
    
    RETURN COALESCE(NEW, OLD);
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

-- Apply audit triggers to sensitive tables
CREATE TRIGGER orders_audit_trigger
    AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OR DELETE ON orders
    FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION audit_trigger();

6.2.4.5 Batch Processing Approach

Batch processing optimizes bulk operations and reduces database load through efficient data processing patterns.

Batch Processing Implementation

// Batch order processing
async function processBatchOrders(orders: OrderData[]) {
  const batchSize = 1000;
  const batches = chunk(orders, batchSize);
  
  for (const batch of batches) {
    await prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
      // Batch insert orders
      await tx.order.createMany({
        data: batch.map(order => ({
          storeId: order.storeId,
          orderNumber: order.orderNumber,
          status: order.status,
          totalAmount: order.totalAmount,
          customerData: order.customerData,
          orderDate: order.orderDate
        })),
        skipDuplicates: true
      });
      
      // Batch insert order items
      const orderItems = batch.flatMap(order => 
        order.items.map(item => ({
          orderId: order.id,
          productId: item.productId,
          name: item.name,
          quantity: item.quantity,
          unitPrice: item.unitPrice,
          totalPrice: item.totalPrice
        }))
      );
      
      await tx.orderItem.createMany({
        data: orderItems
      });
    });
  }
}

// Next.js 14 Route Handler Implementation
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import { prisma } from '@/lib/prisma';

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  try {
    const searchParams = request.nextUrl.searchParams;
    const storeId = searchParams.get('storeId');
    
    const orders = await prisma.order.findMany({
      where: storeId ? { storeId } : {},
      include: {
        store: true,
        items: true
      },
      orderBy: { createdAt: 'desc' }
    });
    
    return NextResponse.json({ orders });
  } catch (error) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: 'Failed to fetch orders' },
      { status: 500 }
    );
  }
}

export async function POST(request: NextRequest) {
  try {
    const body = await request.json();
    
    const order = await prisma.order.create({
      data: {
        storeId: body.storeId,
        orderNumber: body.orderNumber,
        status: body.status,
        totalAmount: body.totalAmount,
        customerData: body.customerData,
        items: {
          create: body.items
        }
      },
      include: { items: true }
    });
    
    return NextResponse.json({ order }, { status: 201 });
  } catch (error) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: 'Failed to create order' },
      { status: 400 }
    );
  }
}

JWT Authentication Implementation

// Authentication middleware
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from 'next/server';

export async function authenticateToken(request: NextRequest) {
  const authHeader = request.headers.get('authorization');
  const token = authHeader && authHeader.split(' ')[1];

  if (!token) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: 'Access token required' },
      { status: 401 }
    );
  }

  try {
    const decoded = jwt.verify(token, process.env.JWT_SECRET!) as any;
    return { user: decoded };
  } catch (error) {
    return NextResponse.json(
      { error: 'Invalid token' },
      { status: 403 }
    );
  }
}

// Protected route example
export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  const authResult = await authenticateToken(request);
  if (authResult instanceof NextResponse) {
    return authResult; // Return error response
  }

  // Continue with authenticated request
  const { user } = authResult;
  // ... route logic
}

// Authorization middleware
export function requireRole(allowedRoles: string[]) {
  return async (request: NextRequest, user: any) => {
    if (!allowedRoles.includes(user.role)) {
      return NextResponse.json(
        { error: 'Insufficient permissions' },
        { status: 403 }
      );
    }
    return null; // Authorization passed
  };
}

export function requireStoreAccess(storeId: string) {
  return async (request: NextRequest, user: any) => {
    if (user.role === 'ADMIN') return null; // Admin has access to all stores
    
    const hasAccess = user.storeAccess?.includes(storeId);
    if (!hasAccess) {
      return NextResponse.json(
        { error: 'Store access denied' },
        { status: 403 }
      );
    }
    return null;
  };
}

6.3.1.4 Rate Limiting Strategy

The rate limiting implementation uses Redis cache to control the number of requests made to a server or an API in a specific period, essential to prevent server overload and maintain the quality of service for all users.

Rate Limiting Configuration

Endpoint CategoryRate LimitWindowImplementation
Authentication5 requests15 minutesexpress-rate-limit with 15 minute window
Order Operations100 requests15 minutesRedis-based sliding window
Analytics50 requests15 minutesPer-user rate limiting
Webhooks1000 requests1 minuteIP-based with signature validation

Redis Rate Limiter Implementation

// Redis rate limiter
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const redis = createClient({
  url: process.env.REDIS_URL
});

export function createRateLimiter(limit: number, windowMs: number) {
  return async (req: NextRequest, res: NextResponse, next: Function) => {
    const key = `rate-limit:${req.ip}:${req.nextUrl.pathname}`;
    
    try {
      const current = await redis.incr(key);
      
      if (current === 1) {
        await redis.expire(key, Math.ceil(windowMs / 1000));
      }
      
      if (current > limit) {
        return NextResponse.json(
          { 
            error: 'Too many requests',
            retryAfter: Math.ceil(windowMs / 1000)
          },
          { 
            status: 429,
            headers: {
              'Retry-After': Math.ceil(windowMs / 1000).toString(),
              'X-RateLimit-Limit': limit.toString(),
              'X-RateLimit-Remaining': Math.max(0, limit - current).toString()
            }
          }
        );
      }
      
      next();
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Rate limiter error:', error);
      next(); // Fail open - don't block requests if Redis is down
    }
  };
}

6.3.2 Message Processing

6.3.2.1 Event Processing Patterns

The system implements event-driven architecture with event emitter patterns where webhook routes emit events and resolve API requests, with event listeners triggering desired processes.

Event Processing Architecture

Event Handler Implementation

// Event processing system
import { EventEmitter } from 'events';

class OrderEventProcessor extends EventEmitter {
  constructor(private prisma: PrismaClient, private websocket: WebSocketServer) {
    super();
    this.setupEventHandlers();
  }

  private setupEventHandlers() {
    this.on('order:created', this.handleOrderCreated.bind(this));
    this.on('order:updated', this.handleOrderUpdated.bind(this));
    this.on('order:status_changed', this.handleOrderStatusChanged.bind(this));
  }

  private async handleOrderCreated(eventData: OrderCreatedEvent) {
    try {
      // Validate event data
      const validatedData = await this.validateOrderData(eventData);
      
      // Store in database
      const order = await this.prisma.order.create({
        data: validatedData,
        include: { store: true, items: true }
      });
      
      // Broadcast real-time update
      this.websocket.broadcast('order:created', {
        orderId: order.id,
        storeId: order.storeId,
        data: order
      });
      
      // Trigger analytics update
      this.emit('analytics:order_created', { order });
      
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Order creation failed:', error);
      this.emit('error', { event: 'order:created', error });
    }
  }

  private async handleOrderStatusChanged(eventData: OrderStatusChangedEvent) {
    const { orderId, oldStatus, newStatus, timestamp } = eventData;
    
    // Update order status
    await this.prisma.order.update({
      where: { id: orderId },
      data: { 
        status: newStatus,
        updatedAt: timestamp
      }
    });
    
    // Log status history
    await this.prisma.orderStatusHistory.create({
      data: {
        orderId,
        oldStatus,
        newStatus,
        changedAt: timestamp
      }
    });
    
    // Broadcast status change
    this.websocket.broadcast('order:status_changed', eventData);
  }
}

6.3.2.2 Message Queue Architecture

The message queue system handles asynchronous processing with retry mechanisms and dead letter queues for failed deliveries.

Queue Processing Flow

Message Queue Implementation

// Message queue with Bull
import Bull from 'bull';
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });

// Create queues for different event types
export const orderQueue = new Bull('order processing', {
  redis: { port: 6379, host: 'localhost' }
});

export const webhookQueue = new Bull('webhook processing', {
  redis: { port: 6379, host: 'localhost' }
});

// Order processing job
orderQueue.process('process-order', async (job) => {
  const { eventType, data } = job.data;
  
  try {
    switch (eventType) {
      case 'order:created':
        await processOrderCreated(data);
        break;
      case 'order:updated':
        await processOrderUpdated(data);
        break;
      default:
        throw new Error(`Unknown event type: ${eventType}`);
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.error('Order processing failed:', error);
    throw error; // Will trigger retry
  }
});

// Webhook processing with retry logic
webhookQueue.process('process-webhook', 5, async (job) => {
  const { storeId, payload, signature } = job.data;
  
  // Validate webhook signature
  if (!validateWebhookSignature(payload, signature, storeId)) {
    throw new Error('Invalid webhook signature');
  }
  
  // Process webhook data
  await processWebhookData(storeId, payload);
});

// Add job with retry configuration
export async function enqueueWebhook(storeId: string, payload: any, signature: string) {
  await webhookQueue.add('process-webhook', {
    storeId,
    payload,
    signature
  }, {
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: {
      type: 'exponential',
      delay: 2000
    },
    removeOnComplete: 100,
    removeOnFail: 50
  });
}

6.3.2.4 Batch Processing Flows

Batch processing handles bulk operations and periodic synchronization tasks with efficient resource utilization.

Batch Processing Implementation

// Batch processing for order synchronization
export class BatchOrderProcessor {
  private batchSize = 1000;
  private processingInterval = 5 * 60 * 1000; // 5 minutes

  async processBatchSync() {
    const stores = await this.prisma.store.findMany({
      where: { isActive: true }
    });

    for (const store of stores) {
      await this.syncStoreOrders(store);
    }
  }

  private async syncStoreOrders(store: Store) {
    let offset = 0;
    let hasMore = true;

    while (hasMore) {
      try {
        const orders = await this.fetchOrdersFromStore(store, offset, this.batchSize);
        
        if (orders.length === 0) {
          hasMore = false;
          continue;
        }

        // Process batch
        await this.processBatch(store.id, orders);
        offset += this.batchSize;
        
        // Rate limiting
        await this.delay(1000);
        
      } catch (error) {
        console.error(`Batch sync failed for store ${store.id}:`, error);
        break;
      }
    }
  }

  private async processBatch(storeId: string, orders: any[]) {
    const chunks = this.chunkArray(orders, 100);
    
    for (const chunk of chunks) {
      await this.prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => {
        for (const orderData of chunk) {
          await tx.order.upsert({
            where: {
              storeId_orderNumber: {
                storeId,
                orderNumber: orderData.orderNumber
              }
            },
            update: {
              status: orderData.status,
              totalAmount: orderData.totalAmount,
              updatedAt: new Date()
            },
            create: {
              storeId,
              orderNumber: orderData.orderNumber,
              status: orderData.status,
              totalAmount: orderData.totalAmount,
              customerData: orderData.customerData,
              orderDate: orderData.orderDate
            }
          });
        }
      });
    }
  }
}

  }

  abstract async fetchOrders(params: FetchOrdersParams): Promise<Order[]>;
  abstract async updateOrderStatus(orderId: string, status: OrderStatus): Promise<void>;
  abstract async validateWebhook(payload: any, signature: string): Promise<boolean>;

  protected async makeRequest<T>(endpoint: string, options: RequestOptions): Promise<T> {
    await this.rateLimiter.acquire();
    
    const response = await fetch(`${this.config.baseUrl}${endpoint}`, {
      ...options,
      headers: {
        'Authorization': `Bearer ${this.config.apiKey}`,
        'Content-Type': 'application/json',
        ...options.headers
      }
    });

    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new APIError(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${response.statusText}`);
    }

    return response.json();
  }
}

// Shopify adapter implementation
class ShopifyAdapter extends StoreAdapter {
  async fetchOrders(params: FetchOrdersParams): Promise<Order[]> {
    const response = await this.makeRequest<ShopifyOrdersResponse>(
      '/admin/api/2023-10/orders.json',
      { method: 'GET' }
    );

    return response.orders.map(this.normalizeOrder);
  }

  async validateWebhook(payload: any, signature: string): Promise<boolean> {
    const hmac = crypto.createHmac('sha256', this.config.webhookSecret);
    hmac.update(JSON.stringify(payload));
    const calculatedSignature = hmac.digest('base64');
    
    return calculatedSignature === signature;
  }

  private normalizeOrder(shopifyOrder: ShopifyOrder): Order {
    return {
      id: shopifyOrder.id.toString(),
      orderNumber: shopifyOrder.order_number,
      status: this.mapStatus(shopifyOrder.fulfillment_status),
      totalAmount: parseFloat(shopifyOrder.total_price),
      customerData: {
        name: `${shopifyOrder.customer.first_name} ${shopifyOrder.customer.last_name}`,
        email: shopifyOrder.customer.email
      },
      items: shopifyOrder.line_items.map(item => ({
        name: item.name,
        quantity: item.quantity,
        unitPrice: parseFloat(item.price)
      }))
    };
  }
}

Gateway Configuration

# API Gateway configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:

data:
  gateway.yaml: |
    routes:
      - path: /api/v2/orders
        methods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE]
        auth: jwt
        rateLimit:
          requests: 100
          window: 900 # 15 minutes
        upstream: http://shopadmin-api:3001
        
      - path: /webhooks/*
        methods: [POST]
        auth: signature
        rateLimit:
          requests: 1000
          window: 60 # 1 minute
        upstream: http://webhook-processor:3002
        
    middleware:

          origins: ["https://admin.shopadmin.com"]
          methods: [GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS]
          
      - logging:
          level: info
          format: json
          
      - metrics:

6.4 Security Architecture

The ShopAdmin multi-store order management system implements a comprehensive security architecture designed to protect sensitive business data, ensure regulatory compliance, and maintain system integrity. The security framework leverages modern authentication and authorization patterns, data protection mechanisms, and industry best practices to create a robust defense-in-depth strategy.

6.4.1 Authentication Framework

6.4.1.1 Identity Management

The identity management system provides centralized user authentication with support for multiple authentication methods and secure session handling. These offer built-in solutions for authentication, session management, and authorization, as well as additional features such as social logins, multi-factor authentication, and role-based access control. Session management ensures that the user's authenticated state is preserved across requests.

6.4.1.3 Session Management

Session management implements secure, stateful authentication with automatic expiration and cleanup mechanisms. It involves creating, storing, refreshing, and deleting sessions or tokens. In addition to the above, consider adding functionality to update (or refresh) the session when the user returns to the application, and delete the session when the user logs out

Session Security Configuration

// Session configuration with security best practices
const sessionConfig = {
  secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRET,
  resave: false,
  saveUninitialized: false,
  cookie: {
    secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production', // HTTPS only in production
    httpOnly: true, // Prevent XSS attacks
    maxAge: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // 24 hours
    sameSite: 'strict' // CSRF protection
  },
  store: new DatabaseSessionStore({
    // Database-backed session storage
    connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
    tableName: 'user_sessions',
    cleanup: true // Automatic cleanup of expired sessions
  })
};

6.5.2.1 Health Checks

The health check implementation provides comprehensive system status monitoring with dependency validation. A well-implemented health check allows monitoring systems to proactively detect and respond to issues, preventing downtime and ensuring a smooth user experience. This guide will walk you through implementing a /health endpoint in your Express.js application, covering various levels of complexity from a simple status code to comprehensive dependency checks

Health Check Implementation

Check TypeEndpointDependenciesResponse Time
Basic Health`/health`Application status< 100ms
Deep Health`/health/deep`Database, external APIs< 500ms
Readiness`/health/ready`All dependencies< 1s
Liveness`/health/live`Core application< 200ms

Health Check Architecture

// Comprehensive health check implementation
export const healthCheckRoutes = {
  basic: async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
    res.status(200).json({
      status: 'healthy',
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      uptime: process.uptime()
    });
  },
  
  deep: async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
    const checks = await Promise.allSettled([
      checkDatabase(),
      checkExternalAPIs(),
      checkRedisConnection(),
      checkFileSystem()
    ]);
    
    const results = checks.map((check, index) => ({
      name: ['database', 'external-apis', 'redis', 'filesystem'][index],
      status: check.status === 'fulfilled' ? 'healthy' : 'unhealthy',
      details: check.status === 'fulfilled' ? check.value : check.reason
    }));
    
    const overallHealth = results.every(r => r.status === 'healthy');
    
    res.status(overallHealth ? 200 : 503).json({
      status: overallHealth ? 'healthy' : 'unhealthy',
      checks: results,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
    });
  }
};

6.5.4 Monitoring Implementation

6.5.4.1 Opentelemetry Configuration

First, you need to enabled the the Next.js specific OTel instrumentation by setting the instrumentationHook property to true in your next.config.js|ts file. Now install the relevant package. npm install --save @vercel/otel @opentelemetry/api. And create a file in the root of your project called instrumentation.ts|js. import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel' export function register() { registerOTel('my-next-app') }

OpenTelemetry Setup

// instrumentation.ts - OpenTelemetry configuration
import { registerOTel } from '@vercel/otel';
import { NodeSDK } from '@opentelemetry/sdk-node';
import { Resource } from '@opentelemetry/resources';
import { SemanticResourceAttributes } from '@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions';

export function register() {
  // Next.js OpenTelemetry integration
  registerOTel({
    serviceName: 'shopadmin-app',
    serviceVersion: '1.0.0'
  });

  // Custom OpenTelemetry configuration
  const sdk = new NodeSDK({
    resource: new Resource({
      [SemanticResourceAttributes.SERVICE_NAME]: 'shopadmin',
      [SemanticResourceAttributes.SERVICE_VERSION]: '1.0.0',
      [SemanticResourceAttributes.DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT]: process.env.NODE_ENV
    })
  });

  sdk.start();
}

6.5.4.2 Prisma Metrics Integration

Metrics is a new feature that allows you to monitor how Prisma interacts with your database. Metrics expose a set of counters, gauges, and histograms that provide information about the state of Prisma and the database connection

Prisma Metrics Configuration

// Prisma metrics setup
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';
import { createPrometheusMetrics } from '@prisma/instrumentation';

const prisma = new PrismaClient({
  log: ['query', 'info', 'warn', 'error']
});

// Enable Prisma metrics
const metrics = createPrometheusMetrics({
  defaultLabels: {
    service: 'shopadmin',
    environment: process.env.NODE_ENV
  }
});

// Export metrics endpoint
app.get('/metrics', async (req, res) => {
  const prismaMetrics = await prisma.$metrics.prometheus();
  res.set('Content-Type', 'text/plain');
  res.send(prismaMetrics);
});

6.5.4.3 Postgresql Monitoring

To collect and export PostgreSQL metrics, follow these steps: Download and install the OpenTelemetry Collector. Add the PostgreSQL receiver under the receivers block. Define an exporter to send data to Splunk Observability Cloud. Ensure the receiver and exporter are included in the service pipeline

PostgreSQL Metrics Collection

# OpenTelemetry Collector configuration
receivers:
  postgresql:
    endpoint: localhost:5432
    transport: tcp
    username: ${POSTGRES_USER}
    password: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
    databases: ["shopadmin"]
    collection_interval: 30s

processors:
  batch:
    timeout: 1s
    send_batch_size: 1024

exporters:
  prometheus:
    endpoint: "0.0.0.0:8889"
  logging:
    loglevel: debug

service:
  pipelines:
    metrics:
      receivers: [postgresql]
      processors: [batch]
      exporters: [prometheus, logging]

6.6 Testing Strategy

6.6.1 Testing Approach

6.6.1.1 Unit Testing

The ShopAdmin multi-store order management system implements comprehensive unit testing using Vitest as a fast-emerging alternative to Jest for testing React and Next.js apps, with over 5 million weekly downloads and known for its speed, especially testing large applications. The testing framework provides out-of-box ESM, TypeScript and JSX support powered by esbuild and is frequently used together with React Testing Library for Unit Testing.

// Test data factories
export const createMockOrder = (overrides = {}) => ({
  id: 'order-123',
  storeId: 'store-456',
  orderNumber: 'ORD-001',
  status: 'PENDING',
  totalAmount: 99.99,

});

// Prisma mocking with vitest-mock-extended
import { mockDeep } from 'vitest-mock-extended';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

const prismaMock = mockDeep<PrismaClient>();

});

API Testing Strategy

The API testing strategy leverages SuperAgent driven library for testing HTTP servers, providing high-level abstraction for testing HTTP while allowing access to lower-level API:

// API integration test example
import request from 'supertest';
import { app } from '../src/app';
import { prismaMock } from '../__mocks__/prisma';

describe('Orders API', () => {
  describe('POST /api/orders', () => {
    it('should create new order successfully', async () => {
      const orderData = {
        storeId: 'store-123',
        orderNumber: 'ORD-001',
        totalAmount: 99.99
      };

      prismaMock.order.create.mockResolvedValue({
        id: 'order-456',
        ...orderData
      });

      const response = await request(app)
        .post('/api/orders')
        .send(orderData)
        .expect(201);

      expect(response.body).toMatchObject({
        id: 'order-456',
        ...orderData
      });
    });
  });
});

Database Integration Testing

Database integration testing uses mocked Prisma Client as best practice for unit testing functions that use Prisma Client, replacing the imported module:

// Database integration test
import { vi } from 'vitest';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';
import { mockDeep } from 'vitest-mock-extended';

vi.mock('../lib/prisma', () => ({
  prisma: mockDeep<PrismaClient>()
}));

import { prisma } from '../lib/prisma';
import { OrderService } from '../services/OrderService';

const prismaMock = prisma as any;

describe('OrderService Integration', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    vi.clearAllMocks();
  });

  it('should handle order creation with database interaction', async () => {
    const mockOrder = createMockOrder();
    prismaMock.order.create.mockResolvedValue(mockOrder);

    const result = await OrderService.createOrder(mockOrder);
    
    expect(prismaMock.order.create).toHaveBeenCalledWith({
      data: mockOrder
    });
    expect(result).toEqual(mockOrder);
  });
});

6.6.1.3 End-to-end Testing

End-to-end testing validates complete user workflows using Playwright, a testing framework that lets you automate Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit with a single API for End-to-End (E2E) testing.

E2E Test Scenarios

User JourneyTest CoverageBrowser SupportValidation Points
Admin Login FlowAuthentication, authorization, dashboard accessChromium, Firefox, WebKitLogin success, role verification
Order ManagementCreate, read, update, delete operationsAll browsersData persistence, UI updates
Multi-Store OperationsStore switching, data isolationAll browsersStore-specific data

UI Automation Approach

Playwright will simulate a user navigating your application using three browsers: Chromium, Firefox and Webkit, requiring your Next.js server to be running:

// E2E test implementation
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Order Management E2E', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/login');
    await page.fill('[data-testid=email]', 'admin@shopadmin.com');
    await page.fill('[data-testid=password]', 'password');
    await page.click('[data-testid=login-button]');
    await expect(page).toHaveURL('/dashboard');
  });

  test('should create new order successfully', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.click('[data-testid=create-order-button]');
    await page.fill('[data-testid=order-number]', 'ORD-001');
    await page.selectOption('[data-testid=store-select]', 'store-123');
    await page.fill('[data-testid=total-amount]', '99.99');
    
    await page.click('[data-testid=save-order]');
    
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=success-message]'))
      .toContainText('Order created successfully');
    await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=order-list]'))
      .toContainText('ORD-001');
  });
});

Test Data Setup/Teardown

E2E test data management implements database seeding and cleanup strategies:

// E2E test data management
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test';
import { PrismaClient } from '@prisma/client';

const test = base.extend({
  testData: async ({}, use) => {
    const prisma = new PrismaClient();
    
    // Setup test data
    const testStore = await prisma.store.create({
      data: {
        name: 'Test Store',
        apiKey: 'test-api-key',
        apiUrl: 'https://test-store.com/api'
      }
    });
    
    await use({ testStore });
    
    // Cleanup test data
    await prisma.order.deleteMany({
      where: { storeId: testStore.id }
    });
    await prisma.store.delete({
      where: { id: testStore.id }
    });
    
    await prisma.$disconnect();
  }
});

export { test };

Cross-Browser Testing Strategy

Playwright has emerged as a powerful tool for end-to-end testing, offering cross-browser compatibility and a robust API for Next.js applications:

// Cross-browser configuration
import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './e2e',
  fullyParallel: true,
  forbidOnly: !!process.env.CI,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : undefined,
  
  projects: [
    {
      name: 'chromium',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] }
    },
    {
      name: 'firefox',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] }
    },
    {
      name: 'webkit',
      use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] }
    }
  ],
  
  webServer: {
    command: 'npm run build && npm run start',
    port: 3000,
    reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI
  }
});

6.6.2.1 Ci/cd Integration

The test automation strategy integrates seamlessly with continuous integration and deployment pipelines, ensuring comprehensive testing at every stage of development.

Automated Test Triggers

Trigger EventTest TypesExecution EnvironmentSuccess Criteria
Pull RequestUnit + IntegrationGitHub Actions100% test pass rate
Main Branch PushFull Test SuiteCI/CD PipelineAll tests + coverage targets

Production DeploySmoke TestsProduction EnvironmentCritical path verification

Parallel Test Execution

The system implements parallel test execution to optimize CI/CD pipeline performance:

# GitHub Actions workflow
name: Test Suite
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [18, 20]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: yarn install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Run unit tests
        run: yarn test:unit --coverage
      
  integration-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:15
        env:
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        options: >-
          --health-cmd pg_isready
          --health-interval 10s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Run integration tests
        run: yarn test:integration
        
  e2e-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Install Playwright
        run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - name: Run E2E tests
        run: yarn test:e2e

State Management Boundaries

// Server Action for order updates
'use server';
export async function updateOrderStatus(orderId: string, status: OrderStatus) {
  try {
    const order = await prisma.order.update({
      where: { id: orderId },
      data: { status, updatedAt: new Date() }
    });
    
    // Broadcast real-time update
    await broadcastOrderUpdate(orderId, order);
    
    revalidatePath('/orders');
    return { success: true, order };
  } catch (error) {
    return { success: false, error: error.message };
  }
}

// Client component usage
'use client';
export function OrderStatusButton({ order }: { order: Order }) {
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition();
  
  const handleStatusUpdate = () => {
    startTransition(async () => {
      const result = await updateOrderStatus(order.id, 'SHIPPED');
      if (!result.success) {
        toast.error(result.error);
      }
    });
  };
  
  return (
    <Button 
      onClick={handleStatusUpdate}
      isLoading={isPending}
    >
      Mark as Shipped
    </Button>
  );
}

7.4.2 Form Validation Schemas

Form validation uses Zod schemas for runtime type checking and user-friendly error messages.

Validation Schema Examples

import { z } from 'zod';

// Order form validation
export const orderFormSchema = z.object({
  storeId: z.string().min(1, 'Store selection is required'),
  orderNumber: z.string().min(1, 'Order number is required'),
  status: z.enum(['PENDING', 'PROCESSING', 'SHIPPED', 'DELIVERED', 'CANCELLED']),
  totalAmount: z.number().positive('Total amount must be positive'),
  customerData: z.object({
    name: z.string().min(1, 'Customer name is required'),
    email: z.string().email('Valid email is required'),
    phone: z.string().optional()
  }),
  items: z.array(z.object({
    productId: z.string().min(1, 'Product ID is required'),
    name: z.string().min(1, 'Product name is required'),
    quantity: z.number().int().positive('Quantity must be positive'),
    unitPrice: z.number().positive('Unit price must be positive')
  })).min(1, 'At least one item is required')
});

// Store configuration validation
export const storeConfigSchema = z.object({
  name: z.string().min(1, 'Store name is required'),
  apiUrl: z.string().url('Valid API URL is required'),
  apiKey: z.string().min(1, 'API key is required'),
  webhookSecret: z.string().optional(),
  syncFrequency: z.number().int().min(1).max(60),
  isActive: z.boolean()
});

export const useToast = () => {
  const toast = useChakraToast();

    success: (message: string) => toast({
      title: 'Success',
      description: message,
      status: 'success',
      duration: 3000,
      isClosable: true
    }),
    error: (message: string) => toast({
      title: 'Error',
      description: message,
      status: 'error',
      duration: 5000,
      isClosable: true
    }),
    loading: (message: string) => toast({
      title: 'Processing',
      description: message,
      status: 'loading',
      duration: null
    })
  };
};
